{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-mn-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"e8b97f0dc1b89c3cac8019c2a72fb4911f93c4c7200b595cc5fed9112a296ff5","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-mn-class-d:lineage:42","source_registry_sha256":"960e2daa314aff60b32f5124e42324d79615ce2a3ea953a336216b4593c0c910","source_liveness_sha256":"0b70283fc58b1f8ea1822994a92e3ce7ff4b722004376a9cd819180969b6fe1e"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Signal and marking confusables and continuation facts","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: steady versus flashing lights, green light versus green arrow, pedestrian signal phases, X and arrow lane signals, ramp meters, white and yellow line pairs, road layouts, turn and special lanes, warning messages and officer whistles","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: steady versus flashing lights, green light versus green arrow, pedestrian signal phases, X and arrow lane signals, ramp meters, white and yellow line pairs, road layouts, turn and special lanes, warning messages and officer whistles
Confusable pairs among the signal and marking meanings, followed by continuation facts from the road layout captions; only the printed text is used, each block ties to one manual page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec10-R01 | anchor: A01
A steady red light holds you until the light changes, while a flashing red light works like a stop sign, letting you go after a full stop once the intersection is clear. [A01]
Why it matters: group red signals; confusable steady versus flashing red; difficulty high.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-R02 | anchor: A01
A red arrow and a steady red light both require a full stop at the stop line, but the red arrow controls only the movement in its direction. [A01]
Why it matters: group red signals; confusable red arrow versus red light; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-R03 | anchor: A01
Both turns on red begin with a complete stop, but the left turn on red is limited to turning from a one-way road onto a one-way cross street, a condition the right turn on red does not carry. [A01]
Why it matters: group turns on red; confusable right versus left on red; difficulty high.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-R04 | anchor: A02
A steady yellow tells you the light is about to turn red, while a flashing yellow tells you to go through with caution and yield to anyone already in the intersection. [A02]
Why it matters: group yellow signals; confusable steady versus flashing yellow; difficulty high.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-R05 | anchor: A02
A green light lets you go but leaves you to yield to oncoming traffic on a left turn, while a green arrow gives you a turn that should be protected from oncoming or crossing traffic. [A02]
Why it matters: group green signals; confusable green light versus green arrow; difficulty high.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-R06 | anchor: A02
There are stop and go signals for pedestrians: Walk lets them start after checking it is safe, a flashing Don't Walk means do not start but finish if already crossing, and a steady Don't Walk means do not cross and get to safety if already in the street. [A02]
Why it matters: group pedestrian signals; confusable flashing versus steady Don't Walk; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-R07 | anchor: A03
A steady yellow X and a steady downward yellow arrow both tell you to prepare to leave the lane, the first because a lane-control change is coming and the second because the freeway lane will close. [A03]
Why it matters: group lane signals; confusable yellow X versus yellow arrow; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-R08 | anchor: A03
A flashing yellow X lets you use the lane only for a left turn, while a flashing downward yellow arrow lets you drive in the freeway lane with caution. [A03]
Why it matters: group lane signals; confusable flashing X versus flashing arrow; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-R09 | anchor: A03
A steady downward green arrow means you may use the lane, and a steady red X means you may not. [A03]
Why it matters: group lane signals; confusable green arrow versus red X; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-R10 | anchor: A03
Ramp meters are red, yellow and green signal lights on freeway entrance ramps that control the flow of merging traffic, working like intersection signals. [A03]
Why it matters: group ramp meters; prereq for the one-car-per-green rule.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-R11 | anchor: A04
Pavement markings direct and regulate traffic, with white lines for traffic going the same way and yellow lines for traffic going opposite ways. [A04]
Why it matters: group markings; confusable white versus yellow; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-R12 | anchor: A04
A single solid white line says you should not change lanes, while double solid white lines say you must not. [A04]
Why it matters: group white lines; confusable should versus must; difficulty high.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-R13 | anchor: A04
Ordinary white dashes allow lane changes, but shorter and thicker white dashes warn that your lane is ending. [A04]
Why it matters: group white lines; confusable normal versus short thick dashes; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-R14 | anchor: A04
Passing in a no-passing zone is illegal, and a solid yellow line marks where you must not pass. [A04]
Why it matters: group yellow lines; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-R15 | anchor: A04
On a two-lane, two-way road divided by yellow dashes, drivers in either lane may pass, but where one side has a solid yellow line, drivers in that lane may not. [A04]
Why it matters: group road layouts; confusable dashed versus mixed lines; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-R16 | anchor: A05
On a two-lane road with two-way traffic marked so that passing is barred in both directions, nobody may pass whichever way they are driving. [A05]
Why it matters: group road layouts; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec10-R17 | anchor: A05
A multilane road with traffic in both directions may be separated by a solid traffic divider, and such a road has no shoulders at its inner edges. [A05]
Why it matters: group road layouts; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec10-R18 | anchor: A06
A center turn lane is marked by parallel solid and dashed yellow lines, while a reversible lane is bounded by dashed double yellow lines that need a green overhead arrow or a sign before you cross. [A06]
Why it matters: group special lanes; confusable center turn versus reversible; difficulty high.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-R19 | anchor: A06
On a three-lane road with traffic in both directions, the center lane is reserved for drivers turning left from either direction. [A06]
Why it matters: group special lanes; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-R20 | anchor: A06
Carpool lanes may be separated from other freeway lanes by combinations of white or yellow lines. [A06]
Why it matters: group carpool lanes; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-R21 | anchor: A06
Words painted on the pavement, such as School Zone Ahead, warn of conditions ahead. [A06]
Why it matters: group warning markings; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-R22 | anchor: A06
A long whistle blast with a raised palm means stop, and a series of short blasts with a hand motion means go. [A06]
Why it matters: group traffic officers; confusable long versus short blasts; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-R23 | anchor: A06
Law enforcement officers, and on some occasions other individuals, direct traffic, and when an officer is present the officer's hand signals come before signals, signs and pavement markings. [A06]
Why it matters: group traffic officers; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]
